title: Present time
subtitle: Present simple, present continuous, present perfect simple, present perfect continuous, stative verbs

rows.example: Noah **cycles** to college.
Lara **doesn't call** us very often.
Priya **works** in a design studio.
**Do** you **have** a valid visa?
Water **boils** at 100°C.

blocks.text: We can also use **do/does** in present simple statements for emphasis.
blocks.note: I **do enjoy** long train journeys. · The shop isn't cheaper, but it **does stay** open later.

rows.example: Maya **is walking** to the station at the moment.
Delivery drivers **aren't stopping** on this street because of the roadworks.
**Are** they **staying** with relatives during the festival?
Remote work **is becoming** more common.
Dad **is always taking** my charger when I need it!

rows.use: Situations that started in the past and are still true
rows.example: She's **had** that scooter for over five years.

rows.use: A series of actions continuing up to now
rows.example: We've **travelled** by ferry, coach and tram — all in the last twenty-four hours!

rows.use: Completed actions at a time in the past which is not mentioned
rows.example: **Have** you **ever ridden** in a cable car?

rows.use: Completed actions where the important thing is the present result
rows.example: I've **booked** the train tickets.

blocks.text: Phrases such as **it's the first / second / etc. time** … are followed by the present perfect simple.
blocks.note: It's the second time I've **been** on a ferry.

items: American English often uses the **past simple** where British English uses the **present perfect simple**: US *I already saw that exhibition.* · UK *I've already seen that exhibition.*

American English uses **gotten** as the past participle of **get**, except when **get** means 'have' or 'possess'. British English uses **got**: US *We've already gotten him a jacket.* · UK *We've already got him a jacket.*

rows.use: Actions continuing up to the present moment
rows.example: We **have been driving** for hours. Can't we stop soon?

rows.use: Actions stopping just before the present moment
rows.example: I'm out of breath because I've **been running** to get here on time.

blocks.text: The present perfect continuous is often used with {pill:all day} {pill:all week} {pill:for} {pill:since} {pill:just}.
The present perfect continuous is **not** normally used with **ever** and **never**.
blocks.note: Have you **ever flown** in a glider before? (not *Have you ever been flying …*)

blocks.intro: Sometimes there is little difference in meaning; sometimes there is a difference.
items: I **have worked** at the gallery for four years. = I **have been working** at the gallery for four years.
I **have read** that guidebook about the islands. (I have finished it.)
I **have been reading** that guidebook about the islands. (I have not finished it.)

blocks.text: Stative verbs are not normally used in continuous tenses because they do not describe actions.

rows.example: **believe, imagine, know, mean, think, understand**
**be, exist**
**hate, like, love, need, prefer, satisfy, want**
**hear, see, smell, sound, taste**
**appear, look, resemble, seem**
**belong to, consist of, have, include, involve, own**

blocks.text: Some verbs (such as **be, have, imagine, look, see, smell, taste, think**) are stative with one meaning and non-stative with another.
blocks.note: **Do you have** your boarding pass with you? (possession) · **Are you having** lunch at the moment? (action: eating)
